questions.title: What makes prior sightings of the same gun “intrinsic” evidence rather than Rule 404(b) propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: The panel affirmed allowing D.F. and C.F. to testify that they had seen Cutbank with the sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle before the night in question, calling it intrinsic evidence relevant to continuous possession and citing United States v. Battle. I'm confused about the boundary between intrinsic evidence and 404(b) 'other acts' propensity evidence. Why is prior possession of the same weapon considered intrinsic rather than a prior bad act offered to show character? What factors does the Eighth Circuit look at (same weapon, temporal proximity, narrative completeness) to label such evidence intrinsic, and how is that consistent with Rule 404(b)'s prohibition on propensity reasoning?

questions.title: How does the Eighth Circuit’s 'context for police conduct' rationale avoid hearsay and Confrontation Clause problems?
questions.question_body: The defense sought a pretrial instruction limiting the jury’s use of D.F.’s statements to police until she testified, invoking hearsay and the Confrontation Clause. The court declined, accepting the government’s position that officers would use the statements only to explain their actions. Why is this 'context' use not hearsay (given it still communicates accusatory content to the jury), and how does the Confrontation Clause analysis treat such testimony? Are there Eighth Circuit guardrails to prevent 'backdoor hearsay' when officers recount out-of-court statements 'for context'?

questions.title: When must a district court give a contemporaneous limiting instruction, and why wasn’t one required here?
questions.question_body: The panel cited Bennett for the proposition that the court need not instruct the jury about each item of evidence at the time it’s admitted if an appropriate instruction is provided at the close of trial. What are the circumstances in which failure to give a contemporaneous limiting instruction is an abuse of discretion? Here, why did the court find no error in deferring or omitting an immediate instruction regarding D.F.’s statements, and what record factors typically drive that determination?

questions.title: Was the harmless-error framework correctly applied given the potential constitutional nature of some claims?
questions.question_body: The court said it would reverse only if the jury was 'substantially swayed' by improperly admitted evidence (DeMarce), then concluded any errors were harmless. If the alleged error implicated the Confrontation Clause (a constitutional error), shouldn’t the standard be 'harmless beyond a reasonable doubt' under Chapman? How does the Eighth Circuit decide which harmless-error standard applies when the court first declares 'no hearsay was admitted' but addresses harmlessness in the alternative?

questions.title: Why couldn’t defense counsel read from the police report to impeach C.F., and what authentication was missing?
questions.question_body: The trial court barred defense counsel from reading portions of a police report during cross of C.F., reasoning there was no proper foundation because C.F. didn’t author the report. The panel cited Cumbie about authenticating extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements. Can someone explain precisely what foundation/authentication was lacking? Could counsel have used Rule 613(b) (extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements), Rule 803(6) (business records), or called the officer who drafted the report? What’s the right way to get that impeachment before the jury in the Eighth Circuit?

questions.title: How does the court reconcile 'continuous possession' probative value with Rule 403 unfair prejudice concerns?
questions.question_body: The opinion accepts testimony that D.F. and C.F. had seen the rifle multiple times before as intrinsic and relevant to possession. But repeated mentions risk propensity inferences ('once a gun possessor, always a gun possessor'). How does the Eighth Circuit balance the probative value of showing identity/ownership of the same gun against the danger of unfair prejudice or confusion under Rule 403? Did the district court need to give a limiting instruction tailored to this risk?

questions.title: What exactly did the jury have to find about prior convictions to trigger ACCA after recent Supreme Court cases?
questions.question_body: The panel states the 'jury convicted ... of being previously convicted of at least three violent felonies,' triggering § 924(e). Post-Wooden and Erlinger, some facts (like whether offenses occurred on different 'occasions') require jury findings beyond a reasonable doubt, but Almendarez-Torres still allows judicial fact-finding on the fact of a prior conviction. What ACCA-related facts did the jury actually have to find here (violent-felony status? occasions?), and which remain legal determinations for the judge? Why frame it as the jury convicting on 'being previously convicted' rather than a judicial finding?

questions.title: Did the panel apply the correct standards of review to the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) 'in connection with' enhancement?
questions.question_body: The court cited Dunn for the standard of review and said the district court did not 'clearly err' in finding the gun was used in connection with another felony. My understanding is that guideline application often involves mixed questions: factual findings (clear error) and the legal interpretation of 'in connection with' (de novo). Did the panel conflate factual and legal components, or is Eighth Circuit precedent to review the 'in connection with' determination as a factual finding when the facts are undisputed?

questions.title: Can unobjected-to PSR facts alone support a § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement for 'another felony offense'?
questions.question_body: The panel emphasized that the district court adopted PSR facts 'without objection,' and on that basis found the gun was used in connection with another felony. Under Rule 32(i)(3) and Eighth Circuit practice, does failure to object equal admission for sentencing purposes? Is there any limit on relying solely on unobjected PSR assertions to establish the 'in connection with' element, given the preponderance standard and due process concerns?

questions.title: Does using a firearm to commit assaults/false imprisonment qualify as 'in connection with' under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B)?
questions.question_body: Application Note 14(A) often focuses on facilitation or emboldening. Here, the firearm allegedly was used to hold D.F. in a closet, threaten her, and assault her while committing other felonies. Is that per se sufficient to satisfy 'in connection with' because the gun facilitated those separate felonies by enabling threats/force? Are there Eighth Circuit cases distinguishing mere contemporaneous possession from possession that 'facilitates' non-firearm felonies like assault or kidnapping?

questions.title: Why is a within-Guidelines sentence presumed reasonable on appeal despite § 3553(a)’s parsimony clause?
questions.question_body: The court applied a presumption of reasonableness to a within-Guidelines sentence (Goodhouse), even though the defendant argued the enhancement conflicted with § 3553(a)’s 'sufficient but not greater than necessary' principle. How does this appellate presumption square with the parsimony clause? What types of arguments or record showings typically overcome the presumption in the Eighth Circuit, especially where the Guidelines are driven by enhancements like § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B)?

questions.title: Did the district court need to make explicit § 3553(a) findings to reject Cutbank’s variance argument?
questions.question_body: The panel said the court reviewed the PSR and memoranda, noted § 3553(a) factors that could warrant a variance, and thus was presumed to have considered and rejected the defense’s arguments (citing Masood and Maluoth). When does Eighth Circuit law require more explicit discussion of particular § 3553(a) factors or arguments (e.g., mitigation, unwarranted disparities, overstatement of criminal history) to allow meaningful appellate review?

questions.title: How does cumulative-error review operate when individual evidentiary rulings are harmless or non-errors?
questions.question_body: The court cited Keys to say it won’t overturn a conviction based on cumulative effect absent substantial prejudice. If each ruling is either not error or harmless, how can the cumulative-error doctrine ever provide relief? What threshold showing of combined prejudice is required in the Eighth Circuit, and how is it assessed when many rulings involve similar themes (e.g., prior sightings of the gun)?

questions.title: What appellate jurisdiction and briefing rules explain the court’s admonition that the government 'expanded the issues'?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes the government framed an issue on appeal that the defendant hadn’t raised, and the court 'did not appreciate' that. In a criminal defendant’s appeal (jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291/§ 3742), what limits apply to an appellee’s ability to broaden issues absent a cross-appeal? Is this tied to the 'cross-appeal rule' barring enlargement of the judgment, or a prudential rule against raising new issues not briefed by the appellant?

questions.title: Does the NFA definition of 'sawed-off' firearm under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(a) automatically trigger § 2K2.1’s higher base offense level, and how is that status proved?
questions.question_body: The PSR set a base offense level of 26 because the offense involved a sawed-off firearm described in § 5845(a). What evidentiary showing is required to classify a rifle as a 'short-barreled rifle' under § 5845(a) at sentencing (e.g., barrel/overall length measurements, expert testimony, photos), and is judicial fact-finding by a preponderance sufficient? Are there Eighth Circuit cases addressing disputes over NFA status for § 2K2.1(a) determinations?
